concepts.name: Aspect-preserving image placement on the unit square
concepts.definition: Drawing an image inside the [0, 1] square scaled by its longer side and centred, leaving padding bands on the shorter side.
concepts.intuition: The same 'photo centred on a square sheet' picture used to normalize the boxes.
concepts.technical: `hpad = (1 − H/W)/2` if W > H, `wpad = (1 − W/H)/2` if H > W; `extent = [wpad, 1 − wpad, 1 − hpad, hpad]`.
concepts.significance: Makes images and normalized boxes share one coordinate system.
concepts.example: A 640 × 480 photo: hpad = 0.125, image occupies y ∈ [0.125, 0.875].
concepts.misconception: That the image is stretched to fill the square — it keeps its aspect ratio.

concepts.name: Labelled bounding box drawing
concepts.definition: An outline rectangle plus a coloured text label at the box's top-left corner.
concepts.intuition: Like a sticky name tag placed on the top edge of each frame.
concepts.technical: `ax.text(x, y, text, c="white", size=10, va="bottom", bbox=dict(fc=color, pad=1, ec="none"))` — `va="bottom"` puts the text's bottom at y, i.e. just above the box in the inverted-y axes.
concepts.significance: Used to show ground truth here and model predictions later.
concepts.example: The pink 'bicycle' tag at the top-left of figure 12.3.
concepts.misconception: That labels are drawn inside the box — they sit above its top edge.

math.title: Padding and extent in draw_image
math.latex: \begin{aligned} p_h &= \mathbb{1}[W > H]\,\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(1 - \tfrac{H}{W}\Bigr), \qquad p_w = \mathbb{1}[H > W]\,\tfrac{1}{2}\Bigl(1 - \tfrac{W}{H}\Bigr) \\ \text{extent} &= [\,p_w,\; 1 - p_w,\; 1 - p_h,\; p_h\,] \end{aligned}
math.source_text: hpad = (1 - height / width) / 2 if width > height else 0; wpad = (1 - width / height) / 2 if height > width else 0; extent = [wpad, 1 - wpad, 1 - hpad, hpad]

variables.meaning: Image width and height in pixels (`image.shape[:2]` gives height, width).
`hpad`: height of each padding band above and below a landscape image, as a fraction of the square.
`wpad`: width of each padding band left and right of a portrait image.
Matplotlib's [left, right, bottom, top] placement of the image in data coordinates.

math.operations: The image's short side covers $H/W$ (or $W/H$) of the square; the leftover is split equally on both sides.
math.purpose: Place the image on the unit square consistently with `scale_box`.
math.interpretation: `scale_box` added an offset $(W-H)s/2$ with $s = 1/W$ to y for landscape images; that is $\tfrac12(1 - H/W) = p_h$ — the same number, which is why boxes and pixels align.
math.intuition: Centre the photo on a square canvas; padding is half the empty space on each side.
math.numerical_example: For $W = 640$, $H = 480$: $p_h = \tfrac12(1 - 0.75) = 0.125$, $p_w = 0$, extent $= [0, 1, 0.875, 0.125]$. The image is drawn from y = 0.125 (top) to y = 0.875 (bottom). Since `ylim=(1, 0)` inverts the axis, `bottom = 0.875` is indeed lower on screen than `top = 0.125`.

code.title: Visualizing a COCO image with box annotations (continued)
code.original_code:
textbox = dict(fc=color, pad=1, ec="none")
    ax.text(x, y, text, c="white", size=10, va="bottom", bbox=textbox)

def draw_image(ax, image):
    ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(1, 0), xticks=[], yticks=[], aspect="equal")
    image = plt.imread(image)
    height, width = image.shape[:2]
    hpad = (1 - height / width) / 2 if width > height else 0
    wpad = (1 - width / height) / 2 if height > width else 0
    extent = [wpad, 1 - wpad, 1 - hpad, hpad]
    ax.imshow(image, extent=extent)
code.what_it_does: Completes `draw_box` (begun on p.358) by adding a coloured label, and defines `draw_image`, which draws an image file on unit-square axes with (0, 0) at the top left, padded to preserve aspect ratio.

line_explanations.explanation: End of `draw_box`: a text background patch filled with the box colour, no edge, padding 1 point; white 10-pt text anchored with its bottom at the box's top-left corner (`va="bottom"`), so it sits just above the box.

`draw_image`: axes span [0, 1] horizontally and from 1 (bottom) to 0 (top) vertically, no ticks, equal aspect so the square stays square. Callout: 'Draws the image on a unit cube with (0, 0) at the top left'.
Load the image file into an array and read its height and width.
Padding for the shorter side (callout: 'Pads the image so it fits inside the unit cube'). Only one of hpad/wpad is nonzero.
`extent` = [left, right, bottom, top] in data coordinates; `imshow` stretches the pixel array to that rectangle.

code.inputs_outputs: `draw_image(ax, path)` draws on `ax`; returns nothing. `draw_box` draws a rectangle and label on `ax`.
code.algorithm: Coordinate-system setup + placement of a raster image into a sub-rectangle of the unit square.
code.theory_link: Implements in pixels the same aspect-preserving padding that `scale_box` assumed for box coordinates (p.357).

parameters.name: ylim=(1, 0)
parameters.role: Inverts the y axis so y grows downward like image rows.

parameters.name: aspect="equal"
parameters.role: Keeps one unit in x equal to one unit in y on screen.

parameters.name: extent
parameters.role: Where the image is drawn: [wpad, 1 − wpad, 1 − hpad, hpad].

parameters.name: va="bottom"
parameters.role: Text is placed above its anchor point.

pitfalls: Swapping `hpad` and `wpad` or forgetting the inverted y axis makes boxes misalign with objects.
`draw_image` takes a file path (it calls `plt.imread`), not an array — later uses with tensors need a different call.

deeper.title: Checking that draw_image and scale_box agree
deeper.body:
For a landscape image ($W > H$):

- `scale_box` maps a pixel row $y_{px}$ to $y_{px}/W + (W-H)/(2W)$.
- `draw_image` maps row 0 to $p_h = (1 - H/W)/2 = (W-H)/(2W)$ and row $H$ to $1 - p_h$, linearly, so row $y_{px}$ lands at $p_h + y_{px}\cdot(1 - 2p_h)/H = p_h + y_{px}/W$.

Both give the same value, so a box at pixel row $y_{px}$ is drawn exactly at that row. The same holds for $x$ with portrait images.

deeper.title: Reading figure 12.3
deeper.body:
- **Blue 'cat'** box: tight around the orange cat, from roughly x = 0.12 to 0.69 — matching `[0.12, 0.27, 0.57, 0.33]` (p.358).
- **Green 'bench'** box: covers the white wooden bench from the left edge, `[0.0, 0.15, 0.79, 0.69]`.
- **Pink 'bicycle'** box: spans the full width, `[0.0, 0.12, 1.0, 0.75]`; its top edge almost coincides with the image top, which is why the 'bicycle' and 'bench' tags overlap at the top-left.
- White bands above and below the photo are the padding computed by `draw_image`.

The colours are blue, yellow-green and pink because labels 17, 15, 2 were seen in that order (hues 0.618, 0.236, 0.854).

takeaways: `draw_image` sets axes to the unit square with (0, 0) at the top left and an inverted y axis.
The image is centred with padding on its shorter side via `extent = [wpad, 1 − wpad, 1 − hpad, hpad]`, matching `scale_box`.
`draw_box` puts a white-on-colour label just above each box's top-left corner.
Figure 12.3 shows the ground-truth cat, bench and bicycle boxes of metadata[435], confirming the data pipeline works.
Box colours follow the golden-ratio hue order in which labels are first seen.

questions.question: For a portrait image of width 300 and height 400, compute `wpad`, `hpad` and the `extent` used by `draw_image`.
questions.explanation: Height > width, so only wpad is nonzero; extent = [wpad, 1 − wpad, 1 − hpad, hpad].

questions.question: Why does `draw_image` set `ylim=(1, 0)`?
options: To flip the image upside down
So that (0, 0) is at the top left and y grows downward, like image and COCO coordinates
Because Matplotlib requires decreasing limits for images
questions.answer: So that (0, 0) is at the top left and y grows downward, like image and COCO coordinates
questions.explanation: The callout says the image is drawn with (0, 0) at the top left. The image is not flipped (extent accounts for the inversion), nothing is cropped, and Matplotlib doesn't require decreasing limits.

questions.question: Why must `draw_image` use the same padding convention as `scale_box` on p.357?
questions.answer: Because the boxes were normalized assuming the image is centred in a square scaled by its longer side; drawing the image any other way (e.g. stretched) would make the normalized boxes misalign with the objects.
questions.explanation: The offsets are identical: (W−H)/(2W) = hpad for landscape images.

questions.question: Where is each label text placed relative to its box, and which argument controls this?
questions.answer: Just above the box's top-left corner; `va="bottom"` anchors the text's bottom edge at (x, y).
questions.explanation: With the inverted y axis, the text extends upward (toward smaller y) from the corner.

questions.question: What does figure 12.3 actually display?
options: YOLO predictions on a test image
A segmentation mask of the cat
questions.explanation: The snippet draws `sample["boxes"]` from the annotations. No model has been trained, and no proposals or masks are involved — despite the caption's wording.

questions.question: Explain why the cat's box is blue, the bench's yellow-green and the bicycle's pink in figure 12.3.
questions.answer: `label_to_color` assigns hues in the order labels are first seen: 17 (cat) gets 0.618 (blue), 15 (bench) 0.236 (yellow-green), 2 (bicycle) 0.854 (pink).
questions.explanation: Connects the golden-ratio rule of p.358 to the figure.

questions.question: Could you adapt `draw_image` to take a NumPy array instead of a file path?
questions.answer: Skip `plt.imread` when given an array (e.g. check `isinstance(image, str)`), then compute padding and extent the same way.
questions.explanation: The rest of the function only needs the array's height and width.
